extracted.intended_audience: school administrators, Title IX coordinators, legal counsel, and other recipients of federal education funding responsible for Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX pregnancy and parental protections
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards implementing Title IX protections against discrimination based on pregnancy, pregnancy-related conditions, and parental/family/marital status for applicants, students, and employees, including required staff actions and interaction with disability law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on discrimination based on current, potential, or past pregnancy or related conditions (§106.40(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.40(b)(1) prohibits discrimination against any student or employee based on a student's current, potential, or past pregnancy or related conditions; 'pregnancy or related conditions' is defined broadly to include pregnancy, childbirth, termination of pregnancy, lactation, medical conditions related to those, and recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department affirms that recipients violate Title IX by stopping or reducing financial assistance, subjecting students of one sex to additional requirements (e.g., requiring women athletes to sign pregnancy-related contracts), or excluding students from programs or activities on the basis of pregnancy or related conditions. The final regulations update and expand coverage (removing 'false pregnancy') to help reduce barriers to educational access. The Department will offer technical assistance and consider further guidance for K-12 recipients as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions: Treat pregnancy like other temporary medical conditions (§106.21(c)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: In admissions decisions, a recipient must treat pregnancy or related conditions in the same manner and under the same policies and practices as any other temporary medical conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarified language (removed 'or any temporary disability resulting therefrom' and changed 'disability or physical condition' to 'medical conditions') to avoid implying pregnancy is a disability. If a recipient provides, for example, extra time to applicants recovering from surgery, it must provide the same to applicants recovering from childbirth. If the recipient has no policy/practice providing reasonable modifications for temporary medical conditions, Title IX does not require it to provide such modifications for pregnancy—but ADA/Section 504 may apply when a pregnancy-related condition qualifies as a disability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-admission inquiries and parity: no sex-based disparate pre-admission questioning (§106.21(c)(2)(iii) and related provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must not implement policies, practices, or procedures—including pre-admission inquiries—that concern parental, family, or marital status and that treat a person differently based on sex; current regulations prohibit pre-admission inquiry into marital status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to add explicit text enumerating 'current, potential, or past pregnancy or related conditions' or expanded family status language to §106.21(c)(2)(iii) because §106.21(c)(2)(i) and (ii) already prohibit discrimination based on pregnancy and sex-based treatment. The final text uses 'all applicants' (rather than 'such applicants of both sexes') to require questions only if asked of all applicants and to be more inclusive and grammatically correct. The Department acknowledged concerns about privacy and modified §106.44(j) to restrict disclosure of PII.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on sex-stereotype discrimination regarding parental, family, marital, or caregiver status (§106.10 and §106.21/§106.40)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are prohibited from discriminating against or harassing students based on sex stereotypes about parental, family, marital, or caregiver status (e.g., assumptions that mothers will neglect education or should focus on caregiving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explained that discrimination based on parental/family/caregiver status often constitutes sex discrimination because women are more often custodial parents; §106.10 covers sex stereotypes and §106.21(c)(2)(i) prohibits treating parenting applicants differently based on sex. The Department declined to explicitly add 'perceived' or 'expected' in some places because existing language (including 'potential') and §106.10's prohibition on stereotypes already cover such situations; the protections apply throughout a student's participation in the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'parental status' protections applies throughout participation (§106.40(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition and protection for 'parental status' is not limited to the immediate period following birth or adoption and applies throughout a student's participation in the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenter concerns that protections were temporally limited were rejected; the Department also referred readers to the discussion of 'parental status' in §106.2 for further definition. The Department would consider broadening language only with additional information (cost/administrative burden considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable modifications for applicants tied to existing temporary medical condition policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.21(c)(1) requires that recipients treat pregnancy or related conditions and other temporary medical conditions the same, including with respect to provision of reasonable modifications, but does not create an independent Title IX right to reasonable modifications for applicants beyond what the recipient already provides for temporary medical conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to create a standalone Title IX reasonable-modifications entitlement for applicants because of the need to consider costs, administrative burden, and interplay with other legal requirements. If the recipient does not have a policy of providing reasonable modifications for temporary medical conditions, Title IX does not require reasonable modifications for pregnancy; however, when a pregnancy-related condition qualifies as a disability under ADA/Section 504, those statutes may require accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee duty to provide Title IX Coordinator contact information when directly informed (§106.40(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a student or a person with legal authority to act on the student's behalf directly informs an employee that the student is pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions, the employee must promptly provide the Title IX Coordinator's contact information and inform that the Title IX Coordinator can coordinate specific actions to prevent sex discrimination and ensure equal access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duty is triggered only by direct notice from the student/legal representative (verbally or in writing); overhearing or secondhand reports do not trigger it. The provision does not require the employee to notify the Title IX Coordinator, to approach students unprompted, to ask sensitive questions, or to document compliance. If an employee reasonably believes the Title IX Coordinator already knows (e.g., student says they are working with the Coordinator), the employee has no further obligation. The Department changed wording to replace 'for assistance' with clearer language about the Coordinator's coordination role and removed the phrase 'employee is informed' to clarify the direct-inform requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on employee obligations and respect for student privacy and autonomy (§106.40(b)(2) operational limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees are not required to ask about pregnancy, make assumptions about medical status, or act on indirect information; they should act only when directly informed and only if they reasonably believe the Title IX Coordinator has not already been notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a student telling a teacher 'I am pregnant and will be late for a doctor's appointment' triggers the duty; overhearing that statement does not. Employees need not probe whether the student has requested reasonable modifications. The rule balances privacy, autonomy, and administrative burdens; multiple staff informing the student of Coordinator contact info may occur only if the student informs multiple employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and confidentiality protections for pregnancy-related information (§106.44(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any records that a recipient voluntarily maintains about a student's pregnancy or related conditions are subject to the disclosure restrictions in §106.44(j), which prohibit disclosure of personally identifiable information obtained in the course of complying with these regulations, with specified exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasized protection of student confidentiality and noted that the provision does not require documentation of compliance. The disclosure restrictions are explained further in the discussion of §106.44(j). Additionally, recipients may not punish or retaliate against a student solely for seeking or obtaining an abortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with ADA and Section 504 (intersection with disability law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pregnancy itself is not a disability, but some pregnancy-related conditions or complications may qualify as disabilities under the ADA or Section 504; when they do, the recipient must comply with nondiscrimination obligations under those laws as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'temporary medical conditions' may be part of a recipient's disability policy or separate, the Department revised regulatory language for clarity. Where a pregnancy-related condition qualifies as a disability, recipients must provide reasonable accommodations under ADA/Section 504 even if Title IX's reasonable-modifications rules do not independently require them for applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on discriminatory actions that reduce educational opportunities (athletics, scholarships, activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may not take actions such as stopping or reducing financial assistance, excluding students from participation in education programs or activities (including extracurricular activities and athletics), or imposing differential requirements on students of one sex because of pregnancy or related conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reaffirmed longstanding interpretations and cited prior guidance (e.g., Dear Colleague Letter: Student Athletes and Pregnancy). The final regulations maintain these prohibitions and provide broadly inclusive coverage of pregnancy-related conditions and recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of neutral, inclusive phrasing and practical drafting choices (e.g., 'all applicants' and 'implement' substitutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department chose phrasing such as 'all applicants' instead of 'such applicants of both sexes' and substituted 'implement' for 'apply' in certain sections to promote inclusivity, clarity, and grammatical correctness without changing substantive coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explained that 'all applicants' conveys the same point as earlier statutory language limiting inquiries to those asked of both sexes, but is more inclusive and grammatically correct. Small textual edits were made for clarity and consistency across sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of administrative burden and need for additional information before expanding protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department repeatedly declined to adopt broader enumerations (e.g., adding 'perceived' or 'expected' across certain provisions or creating independent applicant reasonable-modifications rights) without further consideration of cost, administrative burden, or interplay with other legal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While receptive to commenters' concerns, the Department balanced expanded protections against practical implementation concerns and legal overlap, indicating willingness to consider additional changes only after further information is assessed.
